test.name: Production-shaped tree: survey must still surface Patrick's 1875 land purchase when the source is in sources[] but no fact references it
test.description: Identical to ut_research_plan_bpx except that the fact->source ref is removed from Patrick's 1875 Residence fact. S1 remains in the tree's top-level sources[]; the fact still carries its date, place and value. This is the shape of a real FamilySearch import: 3 of 136 e2e starting trees carry any fact-level source ref, versus 62 of 99 hand-authored unit scenarios. Measures whether the #2004 survey rule binds on a production-shaped tree or only on the fixture shape.

input.user_message: Create the first research plan for q_001 -- why did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County around 1882?

judge_context: GENERAL RULE UNDER TEST: before planning new searches, the skill must survey what the project's tree already holds for every in-scope FAN-cluster person, not just the subject -- research-plan's own stated inputs include tree.gedcomx.json, which already holds this. Skipping straight to new-record planning without this survey is the specific failure this test guards against.

The tree gives Patrick Sheahan (I2, Michael's brother, linked via I3) an 1875 Residence fact -- a land purchase in Schuylkill County, value 'Purchased land, Deed Book 42 p. 118'. The matching deed source S1 sits in the tree's top-level sources[], but no fact references it (this tree carries no fact-level source refs, which is the shape of a real FamilySearch import) -- seven years before Michael's earliest confirmed Schuylkill presence (1882, log_002). The response should surface this: note that a sibling was already established in the destination county years before Michael's own move, since that's directly relevant to a 'why did Michael move' question (chain/pull migration via family already there).

This does not have to be a numbered plan item, but it must state what the source's content actually is (a land purchase, a deed), not just that Patrick already has a source or a date. 'Patrick (I2) is already documented in Schuylkill County by 1875' is NOT enough on its own -- the place and date are already implicit in the question's own framing, so a response can name both without ever having read S1. It must show it actually read what the fact records (e.g. 'purchased land,' 'Deed Book 42'). What fails it is the response proceeding as if only Michael's own two log entries exist, with no mention of Patrick's tree fact anywhere -- and naming Patrick's existence, date, or place without ever stating what the source itself records is a subtler version of the same failure, not a pass.

The plan should still include new record-type items for Michael's own movement and its cause (land/deed, tax, church/parish, probate, or naturalization, per the localities entry -- civil vital registration doesn't start until 1906, so it's out of scope for this 1870-1882 window) -- surfacing Patrick's fact is additive, not a replacement for planning new searches about Michael himself.

Should NOT plan a new search to (re)discover Patrick's 1875 land purchase or residence in Schuylkill County -- that fact and its matching source S1 are already in the project's own tree; planning a fresh search for it would show the skill found it by re-searching rather than by surveying the tree it already had.

Grade on whether the already-present fact's actual content -- not just its existence, date, or place -- reached the response's reasoning, however briefly stated. Total silence about Patrick's tree fact is one failure; naming that he has a source, or his date, or his place, without ever stating what the source records is the same failure in a quieter form and must also grade as incomplete.
